building.name: Rhode Island Building Code, RISBC-1 (510-RICR-00-00-1)
building.edition: 2021 International Building Code with Rhode Island amendments
building.local_amendments_note: State law bars cities and towns from enacting local building codes (R.I. Gen. Laws 23-27.3-100.1.7, in the state pack), and Providence's codes page points to the state code and the state amendments only. Chapter 5 of the Providence Code of Ordinances (Buildings), linked from the city's Codes & Ordinances page, sits on Municode and could not be opened.
building.quote: According to the State Building Commissioner, the Rhode Island Building Code Standards Committee has completed the regulatory process for the 2021 International Code Council (ICC) codes, including all Rhode Island-specific amendments. This comprehensive update covers all 13 regulations that comprise the Rhode Island State Building Codes, as well as the 2023 National Electrical Code. The new codes will officially took effect on December 1, 2025. [...] The 2021 Rhode Island Building Codes are based on the 2021 International Code Council (ICC) model codes, as adopted with Rhode Island-specific amendments. [...] The RI amendments supersede the ICC ones.
building.state_quote: The Building Code Standards Committee hereby adopts and incorporates as the Rhode Island Building Code the provisions of the International Building Code (IBC), 2021 edition [...] 101.2 Scope [...] Exceptions: [...] 2. Existing buildings undergoing repair, alterations or additions and changes of occupancy shall comply with the provisions the Rhode Island Existing Building Code (Part 7 of this Subchapter) or the State Rehabilitation Code, Part 20 of this Subchapter

plumbing.name: Rhode Island Plumbing Code, RISBC-3 (510-RICR-00-00-3)
plumbing.edition: 2021 International Plumbing Code with Rhode Island amendments
plumbing.quote: This comprehensive update covers all 13 regulations that comprise the Rhode Island State Building Codes [...] The new codes will officially took effect on December 1, 2025.
plumbing.note: The city page does not list the 13 regulations one by one; that the plumbing code is among them, on the 2021 International Plumbing Code, is from the Department of State's rules site (state pack: 510-RICR-00-00-3, effective December 1, 2025).

also_listed: 2024 International Energy Conservation Code, adopted November 14, 2024, with appendices RK and CH

transition.what: Providence allowed a grace period after the December 1, 2025 change, during which applicants could choose the earlier (2018-based) or the new code. State law gives three months after adoption. The city page prints the end date as '3.1.2025', which reads as a typing error for March 1, 2026; parent permits approved under the 2018 codes needed all building permits filed before March 1, 2026. The grace period is over.
transition.quote: Per RIGL §23-27.3-114.3.1. Drawings and specifications: Within three (3) months after the adoption (up until 3.1.2025) of any amendment to this code, the owner or the owner's agent shall notify the building official that the drawings and specifications for a project are based upon the provisions of the code in effect prior to the latest amendment. [...] Projects that received Parent Permit Approval under the 2018 Codes must ensure that all associated building permits are filed before 3.1.2026.

fixtures.basis: Rhode Island law bars cities and towns from enacting local building codes (R.I. Gen. Laws 23-27.3-100.1.7, quoted in the state pack), and the plumbing code adopts the fixture chapter with no changes. Providence's codes page names only the 2021 model codes and the Rhode Island amendments. The state pack's counts stand.
fixtures.quote: For a complete and accurate interpretation of the RI Building Code requirements, both the ICC base codes and the RI amendments must be reviewed together. The RI amendments supersede the ICC ones.
fixtures.confidence_note: The table itself was read by the state agent on a secondary copy (UpCodes); that caveat carries over.

permit.exempt_list_quote: Q: What work can be done without permit? Building: One-story detached accessory structures used as tool and storage sheds, playhouses and similar uses, provided the floor area is not greater than 120 square feet. Fences not over 7 feet high. Oil derricks. Retaining walls that are not over 4 feet in height measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the wall, unless supporting a surcharge or impounding Class I, II, IIIA liquids. Water tanks supported directly on grade if the capacity is not greater than 5,000 gallons and the ratio of height to diameter or width is not greater than 2:1. Sidewalks and driveways not more than 30 inches above adjacent grade, and not over any basement or story below and are not part of an accessible route. Painting, papering, tiling, carpeting, cabinets, counter tops and similar finish work. Temporary motion picture, television and theater stage sets and scenery. Prefabricated swimming pools accessory to a Group R-3 occupancy that are less than 24 inches deep, are not greater than 5,000 gallons and are installed entirely above ground. Shade cloth structures constructed for nursery or agricultural purposes, not including service systems. Swings and other playground equipment accessory to detached one- and two-family dwellings. Window awnings in Group R-3 and U occupancies, supported by an exterior wall that do not project more than 54 inches from the exterior wall and do not require additional support. Nonfixed and movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters and partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches in height.
permit.note: The city's list (the model building code's exempt list; RISBC-1 keeps that section) exempts 'similar finish work' and 'nonfixed and movable fixtures, cases, racks, counters and partitions not over 5 feet 9 inches in height'. Toilet partitions or compartments are not named; the 'partitions' item covers nonfixed, movable ones. The plumbing list allows 'the removal and reinstallation of water closets' without a permit where no valves, pipes or fixtures are replaced or rearranged. The FAQ PDF is dated March 2, 2020 (under the previous mayor); it is still the file the local-rules research cites.
permit.state_law_quote: R.I. Gen. Laws 23-27.3-113.1: It shall be unlawful to construct, enlarge, alter, remove, or demolish a building [...] without first filing an application with the building official in writing and obtaining the required permit therefor; except that ordinary repairs as defined in 23-27.3-102.0 which do not involve any violation of this code shall be exempt from this provision. | 23-27.3-102.0: (a) Ordinary repairs to buildings and structures may be made without application or notice to the building official, but the repairs shall not include: (1) The installation of any siding; (2) The cutting away of any wall, partition or portion of the wall; (3) The removal or cutting away of any structural beam or bearing support; (4) The removal or change of any required means of egress; (5) Rearrangement of parts of a structure affecting the exitway requirements; (6) Alteration of, replacement or relocation of any standard pipe, water supply, sewer, drainage, drain leader, gas, soil, waste, vent or similar piping; (7) Electric wiring; (8) Mechanical or other work which affects public health, safety or welfare. (b) All work not classified as ordinary repair shall comply with the rules and regulations or ordinances of the municipality as to the procurement of a permit for these repairs.

restrooms_city.quote: As of January 2021, all places of public accommodation with existing single-stall restrooms are required to designate them as all-gender. The City has allocated funding to provide businesses and organizations with signs. This financial support deepens the City's commitment to equality, while also ensuring our businesses remain in compliance with state law.
restrooms_city.note: No Providence ordinance adding to the state rule was found (one web search; the Code of Ordinances on Municode could not be opened). The city's own page describes the single-user rule as state law and offers free all-gender restroom signs to small businesses and organizations. The page gives January 2021; the statute as read by the state agent says January 1, 2023 for existing rooms.

parts.name: city
parts.note: No city or county sales tax on goods was found. The local tax read in the statutes is the 1% local meals and beverage tax (44-18-18.1), paid over to the city or town where the meal is delivered; it does not apply to goods such as partitions.

sales_tax.quote: 44-18-18. Sales tax imposed. A tax is imposed upon sales at retail in this state [...] at the rate of six percent (6%) of the gross receipts of the retailer from the sales or rental charges; [...] provided, further, that for the period commencing July 1, 1990, the tax rate is seven percent (7%).

other_quotes.quote: 44-18-18.1. Local meals and beverage tax. (a) There is hereby levied and imposed, upon every purchaser of a meal and/or beverage, in addition to all other taxes and fees now imposed by law, a local meals and beverage tax [...] at a rate of one percent of the gross receipts.

sales_tax.not_done: The Division of Taxation's web pages (tax.ri.gov rate page) return HTTP 403 to automated access, so no Division page stating outright that there is no local sales tax was read; Rhode Island publishes no address lookup that was found. The rate rests on the statute and the Division's contractor guide (PDF, February 2024). Secondary sources seen in search results (Tax Foundation, Avalara) give a 0% local rate.

IN HEIGHT WHEN CONSTRUCTED: $.50 PER HOUR ADDITIONAL. [...]) ...........$ 47.88 30.50
public_wage.note: Modification 5 is the latest (modification 6 returns 404). The Department of Labor and Training's own posting of the rates (dlt.ri.gov) is blocked to automated access; under the state rule the prevailing wage is the base rate plus fringe on the federal general wage decision, with contractors moving to the new rates each July 1 (state pack).

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Providence job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material for New England weather and see the local rules.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Providence colleges, hospitals, offices and restaurants, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Rhode Island's plumbing rules set the number of toilets and urinals by how many people use the building. State law doesn't let cities change them, so Providence applies them as written. The table below shows what that means.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Rhode Island law requires a permit to alter a building but not for ordinary repairs. Providence's list of work that needs no permit covers painting, tiling, cabinets, counter tops "and similar finish work", and movable partitions up to 5 feet 9 inches high. It doesn't name toilet partitions, so ask the Providence Department of Inspection and Standards whether your replacement needs one. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.confirm_office: the Providence Department of Inspection and Standards
page.install_rule: Providence issues commercial building permits only to a licensed contractor, whose Rhode Island Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board registration is listed on the permit. Rhode Island requires contractors who build or repair commercial buildings to register with that board. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A contractor who pulls a commercial permit in Providence must be registered with the Rhode Island Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on state, city, town and public school projects over $1,000, Rhode Island law requires at least the prevailing wage, which the state Department of Labor and Training takes from the federal wage decisions and updates each July 1. For a carpenter on building work in Providence County that is $47.88 an hour plus $30.50 in benefits.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 7% in Providence, which is Rhode Island's state rate. No city or county sales tax on goods was found.
page.buyers_extra: - **Colleges, universities and hospitals:** phenolic or HDPE in dormitory, classroom and public restrooms that see heavy daily use, stainless steel where the finish matters.
